schools.summary: Gill: the king and Haman came 'to drink' the banquet of wine, in answer to the queen's invitation.
Keil and Delitzsch render the coming 'to drink' in the queen's apartment and frame this second banquet (after Esther 5:6) as the ground of the whole reversal to come.
Henry catches the moment: 'the king in humour, and Haman out of humour, meet at Esther's table.'

themes: king in humour, Haman out of humour

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch mark the question and the 'half the kingdom' pledge renewed as at Esther 5:6, the request framed as the price she offers; Ellicott reads the king assuming the banquets only prepared the way for her real suit.
Gill: it was of God that the petition was kept on the king's mind, moving him to solicit it a third time.
Clarke, with the Vulgate, notes the king was warmed with wine and so the readier to grant her measures.
Henry: the king, mindful of her errand, was bound with 'the threefold cord of a promise thrice made.'

themes: the pledge to half the kingdom

schools.summary: Clarke judges the appeal 'artfully as well as honestly managed,' aimed at the king's love; Wesley reads her plea for her life with its pathos — a queen driven to beg.
Gill pictures Esther lifting her eyes to heaven in secret prayer (the Targum) before she speaks.
Keil and Delitzsch note the deferential formula of Esther 5:8 and the long-withheld petition for her life and people.
Henry: majesty and multitude make these lives precious — a crowned head and a whole people aimed at.

themes: let my life be given me
the pathos of a queen's petition

schools.summary: Clarke: not ten thousand talents could compensate the state for the loss of a whole nation; Wesley reckons the loss in the king's customs and tributes from the Jews, which no payment could repair.
Ellicott: the words are the very language of the decree (Esther 3:13); Esther confesses her nationality and stakes all on the king's impulse, the hearts of kings being in God's rule.
Gill hears in 'we are sold' an allusion to Haman's ten thousand talents and the precise words of the decree.
Henry: had they been sold into bondage she would not have complained; it is because they are sold to be destroyed that it is time to speak, persecution being as impolitic as impious.

debates.question: What is meant by 'although the enemy could not countervail the king's damage'?

sides.position: no sum Haman pays can offset the realm's loss from a national massacre
had it been mere enslavement rather than slaughter, Esther would have kept silent, the affliction being beneath the king's notice

themes: we are sold to be destroyed

schools.summary: Clarke renders the broken Hebrew word for word as the mark of a mind struck by a diabolical plot; Wesley hears speech 'short and doubled' from an enraged mind, and notes the king startles at an evil he himself consented to.
Keil and Delitzsch read the repeated verb as excited indignation, and trace the deed to the heart that fills the man (Matt. 15:19; Eccles. 8:11).
Gill: the doubled 'said' expresses the ruffle of the king's wrathful mind, not (with Jarchi) a first direct address.
Henry: the king is amazed at a wickedness he is himself chargeable with, having sealed the edict — 'Thou art the man' Esther might have said.

themes: Who is he, and where is he?

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott render the word for Haman's terror as a shrinking back in dread (cf. Dan. 8:17; 1 Chr. 21:30).
Wesley: it was time to fear, the queen his prosecutor, the king his judge, his conscience a witness.
Gill: Haman was adversary to the king too, drawing him to loss of revenue; Esther names him to his face, leaving him room to clear himself.
Henry: Esther charges him to his face; he is 'cast into a net by his own feet,' in straits at the height of his sufficiency.

themes: the adversary and enemy is this wicked Haman

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch mark the pregnant 'arose into the garden' and the doom already 'determined' (cf. 1 Sam. 20:7); Ellicott glosses the phrase 'the evil, the doom.'
Gill: the king could not bear the sight of Haman and withdrew to cool his wrath and consider his punishment.
Wesley: the king went out disdaining the sight of so audacious a man, his going showing the commotion of his mind.
Henry: the king vexed at himself and at Haman; the great reversal — Haman abject at Esther's feet, God scattering the proud (Luke 1:51; Rev. 3:9).

themes: the king storms to the garden
Haman a suppliant at Esther's feet

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch fix the tableau — Haman fallen on Esther's couch — and the sentence of death passed without explanation; Ellicott weighs the king's own base character even as God makes him the blind instrument of deliverance.
Clarke gives the Roman lictor's formula for covering a condemned man's head; Wesley reads the king's words not as real jealousy but as the venting of an exasperated mind.
Gill: the king returned a little cooler and more composed.
Henry: the king had no real suspicion but seized the posture to loose his passion; the servants covered Haman's face for execution.

outliers.note: Turns aside to indict Ahasuerus himself — base and worthless, ignoring his own consent to the massacre — while allowing that God works great ends through unholy instruments.

themes: the covered face of the condemned

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: Harbonah (Esther 1:10) points to the gallows 'also,' the other eunuchs having already accused Haman; Mordecai had 'spoken good for the king' (Esther 2:22); Ellicott hears the book's climax and notes Haman falls in sight of his own household.
Clarke turns it to retribution — 'Harm watch, harm catch,' and Perillus burnt in his own brazen bull; the contrivers of death perish by their own invention.
Gill names Harbonah one of the seven chamberlains (Josephus: Sabouchadas).
Henry: the courtiers turn on the fallen favourite — the chamberlain who fetched him now informs against him — filling up the measure of his iniquity.

outliers.note: Reads Haman's fall typologically — a figure of the Saviour treading down the foe, and of the Lamb's victory over sin and Satan.

themes: the snare closes on its maker

schools.summary: Henry reads the execution in three heads — pride brought down, persecution punished, mischief returned on its contriver (Ps. 7:15-16) — the tables turned, Mordecai the crown and Haman the cross.
Gill weighs the place of hanging — Haman's courtyard, or beyond the city gates per the apocryphal supplement.
Keil and Delitzsch record the bare fact: Haman hanged, and the king's wrath pacified.
